description: We’re a group of students interested in software, space exploration, data, and design! Our team has experience with web development, programming, data visualization, graphic design, and hackathons.
summary: Hi! We're the team at Voyager Z, and we designed a tool called Eclipse, which is an interactive navigator for identifying and exploring potential landing sites on the Moon. Our application integrates NASA’s data about the topography of the Moon as well as the computations regarding the positions of the Sun and the Earth in order to provide visual representation of the conditions at a variety of times and places. By integrating such factors as sunlight and visibility of Earth as well as their comparison with each other into an easily accessible format, Eclipse solves the problem of lunar mission planning. The issue lies in the necessity to take into account the amount of sunlight, visibility of Earth and surrounding terrain while choosing the appropriate landing site.
details: Eclipse is a navigational tool that enables users to explore and compare conditions at different lunar landing sites. NASA already provides data through tools such as JPL Horizons and NAIF SPICE, but using them requires specialist knowledge and working across separate tools. This can make lunar exploration less accessible to hobbyists, students, educators, and professionals outside the field. Eclipse brings this information together in a more accessible interface. Users can choose from 23 real sites, including NASA’s south pole candidates, recent landers such as Chandrayaan 3, and all six Apollo landings, or click anywhere on the Moon. They can select any time period and mission duration from 2026 through 2028 and explore the 3D terrain around the landing site. Eclipse shows the amount of sunlight available, visibility of Earth, future variations in these parameters, estimated energy, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset. Eclipse also lets users compare landing sites and times side by side and explore possible landing windows. Communication features model links in S, X, and Ka bands to five ground stations in Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra, Malargüe, and Usuda, showing how radio frequency affects transmission and how rainfall weakens the signal, especially in Ka band. Users can even simulate sending a photo to Earth with the approximately 1.3-second signal delay, walk/roam around as the astronaut or a rover for a more intricate and textured feel of the landing site, and hide the UI for a photo/video mode to take stunning 4k media of their findings and project/mission details. Our group took into consideration rugged terrain, variations in sunlight, visibility of Earth, communication conditions, and landing times. Eclipse uses lunar altitude data from NASA’s LOLA, as well as NASA/JPL ephemeris DE440 data and NAIF SPICE for Sun and Earth positions. We used Three.js to display the terrain in real time, React and TypeScript to develop the UI, and Figma to design the user experience. We used Python for data processing, NASA imagery downloads, and logo creation. Other resources include LROC imagery, NASA’s Lunar Surface Data Book, NSSDC landing coordinates, SerpAPI, NASA Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons for checking calculations. ERA5 precipitation data from Microsoft Planetary Computer and ITU propagation models support the communication estimates, alongside ESA and JAXA ground station information.
